```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      warning = TRUE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

The code below is the complete executable path for this article. The display
helper reads the table's stored name mapping and changes a copy only.

```{r reader-tools}
library(MIRA)
metric_table <- function(x, columns) {
  mapping <- attr(x, "mira_metric_names")
  actual <- columns
  mapped <- columns %in% names(mapping)
  actual[mapped] <- unname(mapping[columns[mapped]])
  stopifnot(all(actual %in% names(x)))
  answer <- x[, actual, drop = FALSE]
  names(answer) <- columns
  answer
}
display_p <- function(x, columns = c("p_raw", "p_primary")) {
  answer <- x
  for (column in intersect(columns, names(answer))) {
    answer[[column]] <- format.pval(answer[[column]], digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
  }
  answer
}
```

## Question, design, and estimands

This reference is for readers familiar with regression and repeated-measures
inference. A synthetic DME study asks whether study-eye BCVA gains differ
between two hypothetical retinal-treatment strategies after adjustment for
age, lens status and a separate pre-enrolment OCT screening measurement.
BCVA is an ETDRS letter score; more letters mean better measured acuity.
Strategy A and Strategy B are generic teaching labels, not named drugs or
recommended regimens. The four visits are Baseline, Month 2, Month 4 and
Month 6. There are 96 independent adults and exactly one eligible study eye
per adult. Both eyes are assumed eligible in this simulation; the protocol
randomly designates right or left before generating any response.
The unselected fellow eye is not analyzed. No result from this simulation
establishes efficacy or a clinical advantage for an actual treatment.

We distinguish a visit-specific adjusted arm difference, an interaction contrast
that compares changes, and a global hypothesis about an entire set of
coefficients. Their p-values answer different questions. None establishes
clinical importance or transports a synthetic result to a real population.

Read the [first-model article](frequentist-long-first-model.html) first if
random intercepts, model frames, or a model-based mean change are new to you.
It explains one population without adjustment. This article changes the
question to an adjusted comparison of two arms and then serves as a reference
for the alternative modules. The [treatment tutorial](frequentist-long-treatment-groups.html)
explains unadjusted comparisons. Here selected covariates affect models;
descriptive tables and paired comparisons remain unadjusted.

## Generate a sufficiently informative study

The new generator uses a baseline mean of about 57 ETDRS letters, patient
intercept SD 7 letters, patient slope SD 1.2 letters per scheduled visit and
measurement-error SD 3.4 letters. Strategy A gains 1.1 letters per visit on
average; Strategy B has an additional 1.5-letter gain per visit. These are
arbitrary simulation parameters, not clinical effect-size assumptions.

`screening_cmt` is an always-observed OCT measure obtained before enrolment:
mean thickness of the central 1-mm retinal subfield, in micrometres. It is a
separate measurement occasion, not baseline BCVA or a repeated response used
twice. The variable name is a local CMT alias for this explicitly defined
central-subfield quantity. A greater thickness in this edema cohort is a
different biological construct from poorer BCVA; OCT thickness is not a
validated substitute for visual acuity. Lens status is Phakic or Pseudophakic.
The three predictors illustrate an explicit scientific working model; their
coefficients are invented and their inclusion is not a general confounder rule.

Scores are rounded to whole letters and checked within an interior teaching
window without clipping. The Gaussian methods approximate the conditional
letter-score distribution and need residual and covariance checks.

```{r model-data}
set.seed(731411)
n <- 96L
eye_map <- data.frame(
  participant_id = sprintf("RA%03d", seq_len(n)),
  study_eye = sample(c("R", "L"), n, replace = TRUE)
)
eye_map$study_eye_id <- paste(eye_map$participant_id, eye_map$study_eye, sep = "_")
study <- data.frame(
  study_eye_id = eye_map$study_eye_id,
  treatment_arm = sample(rep(c("Strategy A", "Strategy B"), each = n / 2)),
  age = round(rnorm(n, 67, 9)),
  lens_status = factor(sample(rep(c("Phakic", "Pseudophakic"), each = n / 2))),
  screening_cmt = rnorm(n, 420, 60)
)
subject_intercept <- rnorm(n, 0, 7)
subject_slope <- rnorm(n, 0, 1.2)
scheduled_months <- c(0, 2, 4, 6)
for (j in seq_along(scheduled_months)) {
  visit_index <- j - 1L
  study[[paste0("bcva_t", scheduled_months[[j]])]] <- round(
    57 - 0.10 * (study$age - 67) -
    0.035 * (study$screening_cmt - 420) +
    1.2 * (study$lens_status == "Pseudophakic") + subject_intercept +
    visit_index * (1.1 + 1.5 * (study$treatment_arm == "Strategy B") +
               subject_slope) + rnorm(n, 0, 3.4))
}
centering <- c(age = mean(study$age), screening_cmt = mean(study$screening_cmt))
study$age <- study$age - centering[["age"]]
study$screening_cmt <- study$screening_cmt - centering[["screening_cmt"]]
visits <- paste0("bcva_t", scheduled_months)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(eye_map$participant_id),
  !anyDuplicated(study$study_eye_id),
  identical(eye_map$study_eye_id, study$study_eye_id),
  all(is.finite(as.matrix(study[visits]))),
  all(as.matrix(study[visits]) > 10 & as.matrix(study[visits]) < 95),
  all(study$age + centering[["age"]] > 18),
  all(study$screening_cmt + centering[["screening_cmt"]] > 200))
```

Age and screening OCT thickness are centered after generating the responses;
their stored values are deviations from the study means, in years and
micrometres. Lens status retains its categorical coding. This changes the covariate reference, while
preserving each participant's responses. It also gives the repeated-measures
ANOVA's time effects a meaningful zero-covariate reference. The original
means are retained in `centering`.

First inspect automatic adjustment choices. Automatic selection excludes
longitudinal, ID, and arm columns; the remaining covariates must meet variation,
cardinality, and total fixed-effect cost limits. Numeric variables with at most
five observed values are treated as categorical. Selection is not a scientific
confounder-selection procedure. Explicit adjustment is preferable for a
prespecified analysis.

```{r covariate-detection}
detected <- mira_info_long(
  study, id = "study_eye_id", time_vars = visits, arm = "treatment_arm",
  covariates = "auto", inspect_only = TRUE, verbose = FALSE
)
detected$config$covariates
```

## Request the model bundle and check execution

`analyses` replaces the five logical switches when supplied. Including
`"model"` requests the primary mixed model and the implemented advanced model
bundle; there is no public switch for fitting only the random-intercept model.
Including `"arm_tests"` enables arm-specific work and the time-by-arm model
terms. Merely setting `arm` while disabling `arm_tests` does not fit the desired
arm interaction. `analyses = "none"` disables these optional modules but leaves
core paired comparisons and the Friedman branch active.

The following single call avoids refitting the bundle for every method. It can
take several seconds. MIRA's current package metadata imports the engines;
individual modules also provide structured availability and estimation checks.
Inspect their status even when installation succeeds.

Compared with the first-model example, this is a new dataset with two groups,
four visits, and three explicitly selected ophthalmic-study predictors. We expect both
within-arm trajectories and differences between them. First inspect the
primary fit, then the contrast matching the question; the later engine
sections explain alternative assumptions rather than selecting a preferred
p-value from many procedures.

```{r fit-models}
fit <- mira_info_long(
  study, id = "study_eye_id", time_vars = visits,
  time_labels = c("Baseline", "Month 2", "Month 4", "Month 6"),
  arm = "treatment_arm", reference_arm = "Strategy A",
  covariates = c("age", "lens_status", "screening_cmt"),
  analyses = c("model", "arm_tests"),
  alpha = 0.05, p_adjust_method = "holm",
  improvement_direction = "higher", stable_threshold = 5,
  verbose = FALSE
)
stopifnot(inherits(fit, "mira_info_long"))
fit$model[c("covariates_requested", "covariates_used", "covariates_skipped",
            "converged", "singular", "warnings", "error")]
```

The table below reads every individual module, including correlation-specific
fits. `performed` indicates that the module returned an available result, not
that its assumptions hold. An error indicates failed computation; a
`reason_skipped` can instead identify a disabled module, absent engine, or
non-estimable analysis. Do not infer the reason from a missing p-value.

```{r module-status}
modules <- list(
  emmeans = fit$advanced_tests$emmeans,
  rm_anova = fit$advanced_tests$rm_anova,
  friedman = fit$advanced_tests$friedman,
  kenward_roger = fit$advanced_tests$kenward_roger,
  rank_longitudinal = fit$advanced_tests$rank_longitudinal,
  random_slope = fit$advanced_models$random_slope,
  gee_independence = fit$advanced_models$gee$independence,
  gee_exchangeable = fit$advanced_models$gee$exchangeable,
  gee_ar1 = fit$advanced_models$gee$ar1,
  nlme_cs = fit$advanced_models$nlme$compound_symmetry,
  nlme_ar1 = fit$advanced_models$nlme$ar1,
  mmrm = fit$advanced_models$mmrm,
  cr2 = fit$robustness$club_sandwich
)
engine_names <- c(emmeans = "emmeans", rm_anova = "afex", friedman = "stats",
  kenward_roger = "pbkrtest", rank_longitudinal = "nparLD",
  random_slope = "lme4", gee_independence = "geepack",
  gee_exchangeable = "geepack", gee_ar1 = "geepack", nlme_cs = "nlme",
  nlme_ar1 = "nlme", mmrm = "mmrm", cr2 = "clubSandwich")
module_status <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(modules), function(name) {
  x <- modules[[name]]
  suberrors <- unlist(x[["errors"]], use.names = TRUE)
  detailed_errors <- if (length(suberrors)) {
    paste0(names(suberrors), ": ", as.character(suberrors))
  } else character(0)
  explanation <- c(x[["error"]], x[["reason_skipped"]], detailed_errors)
  state <- if (!isTRUE(x$performed)) "Not completed: inspect reason" else {
    if (length(c(x[["error"]], suberrors))) "Partially usable: inspect error" else {
      if (length(x[["warnings"]])) "Completed with warnings" else "Completed"
    }
  }
  data.frame(method = name, requested = TRUE,
             package = engine_names[[name]],
             package_version = if (requireNamespace(engine_names[[name]], quietly = TRUE))
               as.character(packageVersion(engine_names[[name]])) else "not installed",
             performed = isTRUE(x$performed),
             status = state,
             explanation = gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ",
                                paste(explanation, collapse = "; ")),
             warnings = gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ",
                             paste(x$warnings, collapse = "; ")))
}))
knitr::kable(module_status[, c("method", "performed", "status")],
             caption = "Execution status; completion does not validate assumptions.")
with_notes <- nzchar(module_status$explanation) | nzchar(module_status$warnings)
if (any(with_notes)) knitr::kable(
  module_status[with_notes, c("method", "explanation", "warnings")],
  row.names = FALSE, caption = "Captured diagnostics for modules with notes.")
```

Here every listed module was requested: Friedman belongs to the core analysis,
and the others follow from the enabled model bundle. The detected per-outcome
adaptations are available in `fit$diagnostics$adaptation`; no request should be
inferred solely from `performed`. The installed engine versions are recorded
in `module_status`. Some modules expose `requested` themselves, while older
containers rely on the call and adaptation record for that information.

Use the following distinctions when investigating another dataset. A disabled
request is **not requested**; an irrelevant arm interaction in a one-arm study
is **not applicable**. A request adapted away for inadequate information is
**disabled for insufficient information**. An unavailable engine or insufficient
version is a **dependency limitation**. An attempted calculation with an error
and no usable result is a **calculation error**. A returned fit accompanied by
missing sub-results or nested errors is **partially usable**. A completed
calculation still requires finite, estimable results and scientific checks;
where diagnostics do not establish a cause, record **undetermined**, rather
than guessing from an absent p-value.

## Gaussian mixed models

The primary model has a categorical visit effect, additive adjustment, a
time-by-arm interaction, and a subject random intercept. It is estimated by
REML using `lmerTest::lmer()` when available, otherwise `lme4::lmer()`.
Fixed coefficients describe the conditional mean; random effects describe
subject deviations. The model assumes independent subjects and a suitable
Gaussian conditional error and random-effect structure. This mixed-model
specification has constant additive covariate effects; the public API does
not expose arbitrary formulas or user-defined covariate-by-time terms for
this model. The ANOVA adapter's different expansion is described below.

```{r primary-model}
if (!is.null(fit$model$fitted_model)) {
  stats::formula(fit$model$fitted_model)
}
```

```{r primary-coefficients}
if (!is.null(fit$model$fitted_model)) {
  utils::head(coef(summary(fit$model$fitted_model)))
}
```

```{r primary-variance}
if (!is.null(fit$model$fitted_model)) {
  as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(fit$model$fitted_model))
}
```

```{r primary-interaction}
if (!is.null(fit$model$fitted_model)) {
  fit$model$arm_time_interaction_test
}
```

The interaction likelihood-ratio comparison refits nested models by maximum
likelihood and compares the interaction model with additive time and arm
effects. This differs from testing one coefficient. Time and arm global
comparisons are also retained in `model$global_time_test` and
`model$global_arm_test`. Covariate adjustment addresses measured predictors
under the specified mean model; it does not establish causal control.

The random-slope module adds a subject-specific slope in the ordered visit
index. It still uses categorical time for the fixed mean. Its ordinal scale
does not become elapsed time when labels say "Month 2". In irregular studies,
that distinction changes the covariance interpretation.

```{r slope-model}
if (isTRUE(modules$random_slope$performed)) {
  stats::formula(modules$random_slope$model)
}
```

```{r slope-diagnostics}
if (isTRUE(modules$random_slope$performed)) {
  modules$random_slope[c("converged", "singular", "warnings", "errors")]
}
```

```{r slope-comparison}
if (isTRUE(modules$random_slope$performed)) {
  slope_comparison <- modules$random_slope[["random_effects_lrt"]]
  if (!is.null(slope_comparison)) {
    slope_comparison
  } else {
    detail <- modules$random_slope$errors[["random_effects_comparison"]]
    data.frame(status = "Random-effects comparison unavailable",
      reason = if (length(detail)) paste(detail, collapse = "; ") else
        "No comparison table was returned; inspect the module diagnostics.")
  }
}
```

When available, the random-effects likelihood-ratio comparison is exploratory: zero variance
is a boundary hypothesis, so an ordinary chi-squared reference is not an exact
calibration. A singular fit indicates redundant or unsupported random effects;
it is not repaired by reporting more digits. Convergence failure, extreme
intercept-slope correlation, sparse cells, and dropped coefficients require
investigation before inference. A successful random-slope fit does not
guarantee a comparison table: failed comparison details are stored separately
in `errors$random_effects_comparison`. The diagnostic above retains that
distinction instead of interpreting an absent table.

## Marginal means and scientific contrasts

`emmeans` evaluates the fitted reference grid. Numeric predictors are held
at their means; categorical predictor levels are averaged with equal weights
under the defaults used here. These are
model-based adjusted means, rather than raw arm averages or an automatic
standardization to the study's observed covariate distribution. With an
interaction present, marginalizing over arms can obscure the scientific
question; inspect arm-specific contrasts.

```{r marginal-means}
if (isTRUE(modules$emmeans$performed)) {
  emm <- modules$emmeans
  simple_arm <- metric_table(emm$arm_time$simple_arm_tidy,
    c("time_factor", "contrast", "estimate", "lower.CL", "upper.CL", "p_primary"))
  knitr::kable(display_p(simple_arm), digits = 2,
    caption = "Adjusted arm contrasts in ETDRS letters; pointwise 95% intervals and within-family Holm p-values.")
}
```

```{r interaction-contrasts}
if (isTRUE(modules$emmeans$performed)) {
  interaction <- metric_table(emm$arm_time$interaction_tidy,
    c("time_factor_pairwise", "arm_factor_pairwise", "estimate", "p_primary"))
  knitr::kable(display_p(interaction), digits = 2,
    caption = "Differences between visit-specific arm contrasts, in ETDRS letters.")
}
```

```{r marginal-change}
if (isTRUE(modules$emmeans$performed)) {
  knitr::kable(display_p(metric_table(emm$baseline_final$tidy,
    c("contrast", "estimate", "SE", "df", "p_raw", "p_primary"))), digits = 2,
    caption = "Final-minus-baseline contrast averaged over arms; this is not the arm-by-time interaction.")
}
```

The `contrast` labels give subtraction direction. Simple arm contrasts compare
arms at a visit; interaction contrasts compare such differences over visits.
`baseline_followup$tidy`, `consecutive$tidy`, `time$pairwise_tidy`, and
`trends$tidy` provide other prespecified families. Polynomial trends use visit
order, rather than measured elapsed time. In the standard contrast tables,
confidence limits are pointwise; adding adjusted p-values does not make them
simultaneous confidence intervals. Native Tukey and approximate Dunnett
summaries are retained separately where supported.

Holm controls familywise error within the displayed family under arbitrary
dependence; BH targets false discovery rate under its applicable dependence
conditions, and BY is more conservative under general dependence. The stored
primary, Bonferroni, Holm, BH, and BY columns support inspection, not selection
of whichever correction gives a preferred result. MIRA does not jointly adjust
every global test, every outcome, and every sensitivity analysis.

## Alternative procedures: assumptions determine interpretation

| Procedure and result location | Engine and inferential target | Conditions and limitations |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `advanced_tests$rm_anova` | `afex`; type-III repeated-measures ANOVA, with uncorrected, Greenhouse-Geisser and Huynh-Feldt tables | Complete repeated profiles under the engine's rules; sphericity matters for uncorrected within-subject tests. Corrections change degrees of freedom, not missing-data bias. Numeric adjustment and between-subject categorical factors are supported. |
| `advanced_tests$friedman` | Base `stats`; complete-profile blocked rank test, Kendall's W, paired Wilcoxon post hoc | Does not adjust for covariates or model a factorial arm-by-time interaction. Completely tied data can make inference non-estimable. Post hoc comparisons have their own pairwise samples. |
| `advanced_tests$kenward_roger` | `pbkrtest`; approximate F tests with covariance and denominator-df adjustments for the primary Gaussian model | Requires an adequately converged, nonsingular fit with positive residual variance. This is model-based inference, not a robust sandwich correction. |
| `robustness$club_sandwich` | `clubSandwich`; CR2 covariance, Satterthwaite coefficient tests, HTZ joint tests | Clusters are study eyes, one per participant here; enough independent clusters and an adequate mean model remain necessary. Inspect reduced-hypothesis diagnostics if fixed coefficients were dropped. |
| `advanced_models$gee` | `geepack`; Gaussian population-averaged models under independence, exchangeable, and AR(1) working correlation | Sandwich inference is asymptotic in independent subjects; few clusters can undermine calibration. Standard GEE is not a general MAR or MNAR remedy. |
| `advanced_models$nlme` | `nlme`; random-intercept Gaussian fits with compound-symmetry or AR(1) residual correlation | Mean and covariance specifications must be suitable. AR(1) uses ordered visit index, not unequal calendar intervals. |
| `advanced_models$mmrm` | `mmrm >= 0.3.17`; marginal Gaussian model with common-across-arm unstructured covariance, REML and Satterthwaite inference | No subject random effect. Requires adequate visit-pair coverage, full-rank design, converged full-rank covariance, and ignorable MAR response missingness conditional on the model. |
| `advanced_tests$rank_longitudinal` | `nparLD >= 2.3.3`; unweighted relative marginal effects with ATS/WTS | No covariate adjustment. Incomplete profiles contribute observed cells under MCAR; general MAR/MNAR is unsupported. Tests concern relative effects, rather than Gaussian mean coefficients. |

Selected baseline measurements are responses in the mixed model and MMRM.
Neither automatically fits a constrained-baseline model or an ANCOVA with
baseline response as a covariate. Incomplete responses are not imputed. Model
rows must be complete for the required predictors, and sample sizes can differ
from those in unadjusted summaries.

The ANOVA adapter follows `afex::aov_ez()`: categorical between-subject
factors form a factorial structure, and within-subject time interacts with
the between-subject factors and numeric covariates. In this example that
includes arm-by-lens-status and time-by-covariate terms. Its mean structure therefore
differs from the additive covariate adjustment in the mixed model, GEE,
NLME, and MMRM. Centering age and screening OCT thickness makes zero their study
means; uncentered numeric predictors would change the interpretation of
lower-order time effects and trigger an engine warning. These ANOVA results
are another model perspective, rather than a pure change of covariance
assumptions. See the [afex specification contract](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/afex/html/aov_car.html).

The study above deliberately has complete responses and predictors.
`study_eye_id` is the MIRA subject identifier; `patient_factor` in native
objects therefore carries study-eye IDs. The one-to-one `eye_map` establishes
that its 96 eye clusters also represent 96 independent people. Duplicated
patient observations from fellow eyes would not satisfy that design. We can
therefore verify the exact subject-by-visit keys against the wide input,
rather than merely compare the fitted row count with 384. A new dataset
requires reconstructing these keys using its actual outcome and predictor
availability. The rank adapter retains explicit unavailable response rows
in incomplete datasets; its finite-response count and schedule row count
then have different meanings.

```{r model-sample-audit}
eligible <- complete.cases(study[c("study_eye_id", "treatment_arm", "age", "lens_status",
                                  "screening_cmt")])
expected_keys <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(visits), function(k) {
  observed <- eligible & is.finite(study[[visits[[k]]]])
  paste(study$study_eye_id[observed], unname(fit$time_labels[visits[[k]]]), sep = "::")
}), use.names = FALSE)
sample_rows <- list()
formula_rows <- list()
check_sample <- function(name, frame, model_formula) {
  keys <- paste(as.character(frame$patient_factor),
                as.character(frame$time_factor), sep = "::")
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(keys), setequal(keys, expected_keys))
  sample_rows[[name]] <<- data.frame(
    method = name, observations = nrow(frame),
    participants = length(unique(frame$patient_factor)))
  formula_rows[[name]] <<- data.frame(method = name,
    formula = paste(deparse(model_formula), collapse = " "))
}
if (!is.null(fit$model$fitted_model)) {
  check_sample("Random intercept", model.frame(fit$model$fitted_model),
                formula(fit$model$fitted_model))
}
if (isTRUE(modules$random_slope$performed)) {
  check_sample("Random slope", model.frame(modules$random_slope$model),
                formula(modules$random_slope$model))
}
for (name in c("gee_independence", "gee_exchangeable", "gee_ar1")) {
  if (isTRUE(modules[[name]]$performed)) {
    frame <- model.frame(modules[[name]]$model)
    frame$patient_factor <- modules[[name]]$model$id
    check_sample(name, frame, formula(modules[[name]]$model))
  }
}
for (name in c("nlme_cs", "nlme_ar1")) {
  if (isTRUE(modules[[name]]$performed)) {
    check_sample(name, nlme::getData(modules[[name]]$model),
                  formula(modules[[name]]$model))
  }
}
if (isTRUE(modules$mmrm$performed)) {
  check_sample("MMRM", modules$mmrm$data, modules$mmrm$formula)
}
if (isTRUE(modules$rank_longitudinal$performed)) {
  rank_data <- modules$rank_longitudinal$data
  check_sample("Rank: finite responses", rank_data[is.finite(rank_data$value), ],
                modules$rank_longitudinal$formula)
}
sample_ledger <- do.call(rbind, sample_rows)
formula_ledger <- do.call(rbind, formula_rows)
knitr::kable(sample_ledger, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Engine samples verified against source subject-by-visit identities.")
knitr::kable(formula_ledger, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Stored model formulas; covariance and clustering also define each procedure.")
```

Kenward-Roger, CR2, and `emmeans` operate on the primary fitted model and
inherit that sample. Repeated-measures ANOVA and Friedman require complete
profiles here; their sample unit is a participant, rather than a long row.
This agreement of samples is a property of the complete teaching dataset,
not a guarantee that the methods answer the same statistical question.
The NLME formulas display the fixed mean; both NLME fits also have a
participant random intercept and the residual correlation named in the
method table. GEE uses participant clusters and its stated working
correlation. The rank formula specifies the factorial cells, with repeated
observations grouped by participant in the engine call.

## Change one adjustment value and audit the sample

We have just verified that all 96 people contribute to the complete-data
models. Now keep their responses, groups, and other predictors fixed, but
make the first participant's age unavailable on a named copy. The new
question concerns eligibility, not a different treatment effect: which rows
will the adjusted primary model retain? Overall visit means do not need age,
while an adjusted model using age needs its value for every retained row.
Predict the model's participant and measurement counts before running this
example.

This is one additional justified public model-bundle fit on changed input.
The call preserves the original scientific configuration, and MIRA still
computes the full bundle even though we read only the samples. The existing
`fit` and `study` are preserved; no p-value is selected or reinterpreted.

```{r missing-covariate-sample}
study_covariate_missing <- study
excluded_id <- study_covariate_missing$study_eye_id[[1L]]
study_covariate_missing$age[study_covariate_missing$study_eye_id == excluded_id] <- NA_real_
covariate_missing_fit <- mira_info_long(
  study_covariate_missing, id = "study_eye_id", time_vars = visits,
  time_labels = c("Baseline", "Month 2", "Month 4", "Month 6"),
  arm = "treatment_arm", reference_arm = "Strategy A",
  covariates = c("age", "lens_status", "screening_cmt"),
  analyses = c("model", "arm_tests"),
  alpha = 0.05, p_adjust_method = "holm",
  improvement_direction = "higher", stable_threshold = 5,
  verbose = FALSE
)
stopifnot(!is.null(covariate_missing_fit$model$fitted_model),
          identical(covariate_missing_fit$descriptives, fit$descriptives),
          identical(study_covariate_missing[visits], study[visits]))
covariate_frame <- model.frame(covariate_missing_fit$model$fitted_model)
covariate_keys <- paste(as.character(covariate_frame$patient_factor),
                        as.character(covariate_frame$time_factor), sep = "::")
expected_covariate_keys <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(visits), function(k) {
  eligible <- is.finite(study_covariate_missing[[visits[[k]]]]) &
    complete.cases(study_covariate_missing[c("study_eye_id", "treatment_arm",
                                            "age", "lens_status", "screening_cmt")])
  paste(study_covariate_missing$study_eye_id[eligible],
         unname(fit$time_labels[visits[[k]]]), sep = "::")
}), use.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(covariate_keys),
          setequal(covariate_keys, expected_covariate_keys),
          !excluded_id %in% as.character(covariate_frame$patient_factor))
covariate_sample_audit <- data.frame(
  configuration = c("Complete adjustment", "One age unavailable"),
  participants = c(length(unique(model.frame(fit$model$fitted_model)$patient_factor)),
                   length(unique(covariate_frame$patient_factor))),
  measurements = c(nrow(model.frame(fit$model$fitted_model)), nrow(covariate_frame)),
  baseline_descriptive_n = c(fit$descriptives$n[fit$descriptives$time == visits[[1L]]],
    covariate_missing_fit$descriptives$n[
      covariate_missing_fit$descriptives$time == visits[[1L]]])
)
knitr::kable(covariate_sample_audit, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "One missing adjustment value removes one participant's four model rows while preserving descriptive availability.")
```

The solution is 95 adjusted-model participants (95 study eyes) and 380
measurements, while the unadjusted baseline summary still uses 96 letter
scores. Setting strict_id=FALSE would not restore a missing age or supply a
bilateral-eye covariance model. This exclusion is
complete-case filtering on a required predictor, not imputation and not
evidence that missing age is ignorable. In a real study it can change the
target population and introduce selection bias. The unadjusted rank module
does not use age; its eligibility must therefore be considered separately.

Return now to `fit` and `modules`, the original complete-data study. The
remaining engine tables and optional sensitivity use those 96 participants,
not the age-missing variant. Inspect actual inference rather than assuming
each method succeeded:

```{r alternative-results}
if (isTRUE(modules$rm_anova$performed)) {
  knitr::kable(display_p(metric_table(modules$rm_anova$tidy,
    c("effect", "df_num_gg", "df_den_gg", "p_gg", "partial_eta_squared")), "p_gg"),
    digits = 3, caption = "Repeated-measures ANOVA: Greenhouse-Geisser inference and partial eta-squared.")
}
```

}

```{r rank-global-tests}
if (isTRUE(modules$rank_longitudinal$performed)) {
  knitr::kable(display_p(metric_table(modules$rank_longitudinal$tests,
    c("question", "method", "statistic", "df_num", "p_raw"))), digits = 2,
    caption = "Rank-based ATS and WTS; numerical underflow is displayed as p < 0.001.")
}
```

For GEE, CR2, Kenward-Roger, and MMRM, `TIME` jointly selects all coefficients
involving time, including interactions; `ARM` likewise includes interactions;
`TIME_X_ARM` selects their intersection. These are not main-effect tests
averaged over the other factor. Where coefficients were dropped, read
`effect_diagnostics`: a reduced hypothesis does not recover the original
full-design question.

A relative marginal effect above 0.5 denotes larger responses than the equally
weighted reference over visit cells, and arm-by-visit cells when applicable.
It says nothing by itself about improvement direction. Rank confidence
intervals are pointwise logit intervals. ATS uses the engine's large-denominator
F approximation; WTS uses an asymptotic chi-squared reference.

## Diagnostics, effects, and sensitivity

Residual-versus-fitted and normal-quantile plots can expose patterns that a
convergence flag cannot detect. Here the data include random slopes, so a
random-intercept-only covariance can be too restrictive even if optimization
succeeds. Observations within a participant remain correlated; treating all
long rows as independent would understate uncertainty.

```{r residual-diagnostics, fig.cap="Conditional residuals in ETDRS letters from the adjusted random-intercept model: residuals versus fitted values and normal quantiles. The synthetic study has 96 independent participants and four visits per participant."}
if (!is.null(fit$model$fitted_model)) {
  local({
    previous <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
    on.exit(par(previous))
    residual <- residuals(fit$model$fitted_model)
    plot(fitted(fit$model$fitted_model), residual,
         xlab = "Fitted study-eye BCVA (ETDRS letters)", ylab = "Conditional residual (letters)")
    abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
    qqnorm(residual, main = "Conditional residuals")
    qqline(residual)
  })
}
```

```{r sensitivity}
comparison <- fit$advanced_models$model_comparison
knitr::kable(metric_table(comparison,
  c("model", "n", "n_subjects", "AIC", "BIC", "QIC", "CIC")),
  digits = 2, caption = "Engine-specific fit summaries; not a common ranking scale.")
interaction_rows <- fit$sensitivity$question == "TIME_X_ARM"
knitr::kable(display_p(metric_table(fit$sensitivity[interaction_rows, , drop = FALSE],
  c("question", "method", "n", "p_raw"))), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Selected interaction perspectives; n uses each method's native sample unit.")
metric_table(fit$effect_sizes$paired_cohens_dz,
             c("from_label", "to_label", "n", "cohens_dz"))
fit$effect_sizes$mixed_models$random_intercept
```

Cohen's paired `dz` standardizes change by the SD of differences; it is not an
independent-groups standardized effect. Kendall's W, ANOVA eta-squared, model
ICC, and Nakagawa R-squared answer other questions and use different scales.
The R-squared modules require `performance` and retain availability diagnostics.

Do not rank GEE QIC/CIC alongside likelihood AIC/BIC, or compare arbitrary
REML criteria across differing fixed-effect models or engine conventions.
MMRM's native REML AIC penalizes covariance parameters; its BIC uses independent
subjects. Model-comparison metadata record these conventions. Sensitivity
rows contain raw global p-values and do not form a majority-vote analysis.
The displayed interaction rows reduce the table to one scientific topic,
but rank effects, Gaussian mean interactions, and different covariance
assumptions still prevent treating them as duplicate tests. The full
`sensitivity` object retains method notes and output paths for audit.

An optional second fit removes adjustment while retaining complete profiles.
All participants in this particular study have complete responses, so the
sample stays the same and the adjustment specification changes. With incomplete
data, imposing this restriction would also change the sample. Set the
environment variable before rendering to
verify this computationally additional analysis; no chunk is permanently
disabled.

```{r optional-sensitivity}
run_extra <- identical(Sys.getenv("MIRA_RUN_ADVANCED_VIGNETTES"), "true")
if (run_extra) {
  sensitivity_fit <- mira_info_long(
    study[stats::complete.cases(study[visits]), ],
    id = "study_eye_id", time_vars = visits, arm = "treatment_arm",
    time_labels = c("Baseline", "Month 2", "Month 4", "Month 6"),
    reference_arm = "Strategy A", covariates = character(0),
    improvement_direction = "higher", stable_threshold = 5,
    analyses = c("model", "arm_tests"), verbose = FALSE
  )
  stopifnot(!is.null(sensitivity_fit$model$fitted_model))
  sensitivity_frame <- model.frame(sensitivity_fit$model$fitted_model)
  # Both fits retain the same labels, response direction and teaching band.
  primary_frame <- model.frame(fit$model$fitted_model)
  sensitivity_source_keys <- paste(as.character(sensitivity_frame$patient_factor),
    visits[as.integer(sensitivity_frame$time_factor)], sep = "::")
  primary_source_keys <- paste(as.character(primary_frame$patient_factor),
    visits[as.integer(primary_frame$time_factor)], sep = "::")
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(sensitivity_source_keys),
            setequal(sensitivity_source_keys, primary_source_keys))
  sensitivity_fit$model$arm_time_interaction_test
} else {
  cat("Additional sensitivity fit omitted. Set MIRA_RUN_ADVANCED_VIGNETTES=true to run it.")
}
```

To verify the additional branch, run
`Sys.setenv(MIRA_RUN_ADVANCED_VIGNETTES = "true")` and render this installed
package's source vignette with `rmarkdown::render()`. Record `sessionInfo()` and
the status table, and restore the environment variable afterward. The primary
model bundle above executes in every routine build.

Continue to the [complete research workflow](frequentist-long-complete-workflow.html)
for incomplete follow-up and an auditable report. Consult `?mira_info_long` for
the complete method contracts and primary methodological references.

## Further reading

The engine authors document the
[Kenward-Roger restriction-matrix interface](https://hojsgaard.github.io/pbkrtest/reference/kr-modcomp.html),
the [MMRM mean and covariance model](https://openpharma.github.io/mmrm/v0.3.17/articles/methodological_introduction.html),
and [interpretation of interactions in estimated marginal means](https://rvlenth.github.io/emmeans/articles/interactions.html).
Read these alongside MIRA's configuration and sample diagnostics: an engine's
general capabilities may be broader than the options exposed by this wrapper.


The ophthalmic context is informed by the [DRCR visual-acuity measurement
protocol](https://public.jaeb.org/drcrnet/stdy/149) and the DRCR study of
[OCT thickness and visual acuity in DME](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17123615/).
Those sources motivate separate functional and anatomical measurements; they
do not supply this generator's treatment effects, covariance or five-letter
classification band. The band is illustrative, not an MCID or a clinical
decision rule.
